
# DYNAMICS EQUATIONS

While the model is stochastic, the equations below describe the biological dynamics within a single simulation replicate.
Variability among simulations is not described here because users have full control of stochastic, time-varying parameters.
For example, users manually sample the desired probability density functions to generate Monte Carlo samples of a parameter, or specify the year-specific values of a parameter to create a temporal trend in a parameter.

## Juvenile marine abundance and pre-terminal fishery

Let $N^\textrm{juv,NO}_{y,a}$ be the natural-origin (NO) juvenile abundance and $N^\textrm{juv,HO}_{y,a}$ be the hatchery-origin (HO) juvenile abundance of age $a$ at the beginning of the year $y$ (juveniles represent the abundance of each age class before returning as spawners).

Harvest in the pre-terminal ($\textrm{PT}$) fishery of juveniles occurs in the first half of the year.
Assuming no mark-selective fishing, the kept catch $K$ is

\begin{align}
K^\textrm{NO,PT}_{y,a} &= \left(1 - \exp(-v^\textrm{PT}_a F^\textrm{PT}_y)\right)N^\textrm{juv,NO}_{y,a}\\
K^\textrm{HO,PT}_{y,a} &= \left(1 - \exp(-v^\textrm{PT}_a F^\textrm{PT}_y)\right)N^\textrm{juv,HO}_{y,a}
(\#eq:PTKeptCatch)
\end{align}

where $v$ is vulnerability at age and $F$ is instantaneous fishing mortality.

The realized harvest rate $u^\textrm{PT}_y$ in the pre-terminal fishery is used to calculate $F^\textrm{PT}_y$ such that:

\begin{equation}
u^\textrm{PT}_y = \frac{\sum_a(K^\textrm{NO,PT}_{y,a} + K^\textrm{HO,PT}_{y,a})\times \textrm{AEQ}_a}{\sum_a\left((K^\textrm{NO,PT}_{y,a} + K^\textrm{HO,PT}_{y,a}) \times \textrm{AEQ}_a + (N^\textrm{juv,NO}_{y,a} + N^\textrm{juv,HO}_{y,a})\exp(-v^\textrm{PT}_a F^\textrm{PT}_y)\times r_a)\right)}
(\#eq:PTF)
\end{equation}

To facilitate comparison of juvenile catch to adult catch, adult equivalents (AEQ) discount the juvenile catch by how many would have survived to adulthood had it not been caught (through maturity $r$ and natural mortality $M$):

\begin{equation}
\textrm{AEQ}_a = 
\begin{cases}
1 &, a = A\\
r_a + (1 - r_a)\exp(-M_a) \times \textrm{AEQ}_{a+1} &, a = 1, \ldots, A-1
\end{cases}
(\#eq:AEQ)
\end{equation}

If management is by target harvest rate $u^\textrm{PT,target}_y$, then the realized harvest rate can vary by an implementation error term $I$, where:

\begin{equation}
\textrm{logit}(u^\textrm{PT}_y) = \textrm{logit}(u^\textrm{PT,target}_y) + I^\textrm{PT}_y
(\#eq:PTER)
\end{equation}

If management is by target catch $K^\textrm{PT,target}_y$, then instantaneous fishing mortality $F^\textrm{PT}_y$ is solved such that

\begin{equation}
K^\textrm{PT,target}_y \times (1 + I^\textrm{PT}_y) = \sum_a K^\textrm{NO,PT}_{y,a} + \sum_a K^\textrm{HO,PT}_{y,a}
(\#eq:FishMortCTarget)
\end{equation}

Target harvest rate or target catch can be constant with time, or a function $g$ of abundance, for example:

\begin{align}
u^\textrm{PT,target}_y &= g^\textrm{PT}(N^\textrm{juv,NO}_{y,a}\times\vartheta^\textrm{PT}_y, N^\textrm{juv,HO}_{y,a}\times\vartheta^\textrm{PT}_y, m)\\
K^\textrm{PT,target}_y &= g^\textrm{PT}(N^\textrm{juv,NO}_{y,a}\times\vartheta^\textrm{PT}_y, N^\textrm{juv,HO}_{y,a}\times\vartheta^\textrm{PT}_y, m)
\end{align}

where $\vartheta^\textrm{PT}_y$ is the forecast error (observation error) and $m$ is the mark rate.

Alternative equations are used if mark-selective fishing is implemented (Appendix \@ref(app:msf)).
Modifications for mixed-stock fisheries are described in Appendix \@ref(app:multi).

## Advance age classes

The juvenile abundance in the next year $y+1$ consists of fish that survived preterminal exploitation, did not mature, and survived natural mortality:

\begin{align}
 N^\textrm{juv,NO}_{y+1,a+1} &= N^\textrm{juv,NO}_{y,a}\exp\left(-[v^\textrm{PT}_aF^\textrm{PT}_y + M^\textrm{NO}_{y,a}]\right)(1 - r_{y,a})\\
 N^\textrm{juv,HO}_{y+1,a+1} &= N^\textrm{juv,HO}_{y,a}\exp\left(-[v^\textrm{PT}_aF^\textrm{PT}_y + M^\textrm{HO}_{y,a}]\right)(1 - r_{y,a})
 (\#eq:JuvAbund)
\end{align}

## Recruitment and terminal fishery

The recruitment $R$ is calculated juvenile fish that survive pre-terminal harvest and then mature:

\begin{align}
  R^\textrm{NO}_{y,a} &= N^\textrm{juv,NO}_{y,a}\exp(-v^\textrm{T}_aF^\textrm{PT}_y)r_{y,a}\\
  R^\textrm{HO}_{y,a} &= N^\textrm{juv,HO}_{y,a}\exp(-v^\textrm{T}_aF^\textrm{PT}_y)r_{y,a}
   (\#eq:Recruitment)
\end{align}

Assuming no mark-selective fishing, the retained catch of the terminal ($\textrm{T}$) fishery is:

\begin{align}
  K^\textrm{NO,T}_{y,a} &= \left(1 - \exp(-v^\textrm{T}_a F^\textrm{T}_y)\right)R^\textrm{NO}_{y,a}\\
  K^\textrm{HO,T}_{y,a} &= \left(1 - \exp(-v^\textrm{T}_a F^\textrm{T}_y)\right)R^\textrm{HO}_{y,a}
  (\#eq:TermCatch)
\end{align}

The specified harvest rate $u^\textrm{T}_y$ is used to calculate instantaneous fishing mortality $F^\textrm{T}$, where

\begin{equation}
u^\textrm{T}_y = \frac{\sum_a(K^\textrm{NO,T}_{y,a} + K^\textrm{HO,T}_{y,a})}{\sum_a(R^\textrm{NO}_{y,a} + R^\textrm{HO}_{y,a})}
(\#eq:TF)
\end{equation}

If management is by target harvest rate $u^\textrm{T,target}_y$, then the realized harvest rate can vary by an implementation error term $I$, where:

\begin{equation}
\textrm{logit}(u^\textrm{T}_y) = \textrm{logit}(u^\textrm{T,target}_y) + I^\textrm{T}_y
(\#eq:TER)
\end{equation}

If management is by target catch $K^\textrm{T,target}_y$, then the fishing mortality is solved such that

\begin{equation}
K^\textrm{T,target}_y \times (1 + I^\textrm{T}_y) = \sum_a K^\textrm{NO,T}_{y,a} + \sum_a K^\textrm{HO,T}_{y,a}
(\#eq:CatchTarget)
\end{equation}

Target harvest rate or target catch can be constant with time, or a function $g$ of abundance, for example:

\begin{align}
u^\textrm{T,target}_y &= g^\textrm{T}(R^\textrm{NO}_{y,a}\times\vartheta^\textrm{T}_y, R^\textrm{HO}_{y,a}\times\vartheta^\textrm{T}_y, m)\\
K^\textrm{T,target}_y &= g^\textrm{T}(R^\textrm{NO}_{y,a}_{y,a}\times\vartheta^\textrm{T}_y, R^\textrm{HO}_{y,a}\times\vartheta^\textrm{T}_y, m)
\end{align}

Alternative equations are used if mark-selective fishing is implemented (Appendix \@ref(app:msf)).
Modifications for mixed-stock fisheries are described in Appendix \@ref(app:multi).

## Escapement

The escapement $E$ consists of the survivors of the terminal fishery:

\begin{align}
  E^\textrm{NO}_{y,a} &= R^\textrm{NO}_{y,a}\exp(-v^\textrm{T}_aF^\textrm{T}_y)\\
  E^\textrm{HO}_{y,a} &= R^\textrm{HO}_{y,a}\exp(-v^\textrm{T}_aF^\textrm{T}_y)
  (\#eq:Escapement)
\end{align}

## Broodtake

The escapement from marine fisheries experience en-route mortality and then some proportion may be used for brood.
Hatchery production operates around the target number of annual releases of sub-yearlings $n^\textrm{subyearling}_\textrm{target}$ and yearlings $n^\textrm{yearling}_\textrm{target}$ specified by the user.
For the purposes of hatchery releases, yearlings and subyearlings are only differentiated by egg to release survival in the hatchery.
For example, yearlings have lower egg-release survival if they are released later.
Going backwards, the corresponding target egg production needed to reach the target releases depends on the egg survival in the hatchery:

\begin{align}
 \textrm{Egg}_\textrm{target,broodtake} = \dfrac{n^\textrm{yearling}_\textrm{target}}{s^\textrm{yearling}} +    \dfrac{n^\textrm{subyearling}_\textrm{target}}{s^\textrm{subyearling}}
 (\#eq:EggTarget)
\end{align}

where $s$ is survival from the egg to the corresponding life stage in the hatchery.

From here, there are two ways to specify how natural-origin brood (NOB) and hatchery-origin brood (HOB) are taken to reach the release target:

1. The "parametric" approach constrains broodtake based on a combination of parameters that control: (a) target releases, (b) target proportion of natural-origin fish in the brood, and (c) limit of proportion of natural-origin fish to use as brood. 
These parameters roughly follow the settings used in AHA [@hsrg2020].
2. Custom brood function that allows user to write an algorithm that calculates brood from the return. The code ensures target releases are not exceeded.

_Parameterization 1: Parameteric brood calculation_

Two parameters control NOB and HOB.
First, the target proportion of natural-origin fish in the broodstock ($p^\textrm{NOB}_\textrm{target}$) is specified. 
To minimize genetic drift of the natural spawning population due to hatchery program, it may be desirable to maintain a high proportion of natural-origin broodtake.

This target can be achieved if the mark rate is one (all hatchery-origin fish can be identified in the in-river return). 
If the mark rate is not 1, then $p^\textrm{NOB}_\textrm{target}$ is the target proportion of unmarked fish in the broodtake. Consequently, the realized $p^\textrm{NOB}$ is lower as some unmarked fish are hatchery-origin.
The target also may not be met when returns are low because brood is taken until the release target is achieved.

The second parameter is $p^\textrm{NOB}_\textrm{max}$, the maximum allowable proportion of the natural-origin return to be used as broodtake. 
This value is never exceeded.

From these constraints, the broodtake (non-selective with respect to age) is back-calculated from target egg production based on brood fecundity and hatchery survival of broodstock.

Natural-origin brood is taken from some proportion $p^\textrm{broodtake,unmarked}$ of fish in passage to spawning grounds:

\begin{equation}
\textrm{NOB}_{y,a} = p^\textrm{broodtake,unmarked}_y \times E^\textrm{NO,avail}_{y,a}
(\#eq:NOB)
\end{equation}

where $E^\textrm{NO,avail}_{y,a} = E^\textrm{NO}_{y,a}\times s_\textrm{enroute} \times p^\textrm{esc}_\textrm{max}$ is a subset of the natural-origin escapement reduced by en-route mortality (with survival $s_\textrm{enroute}$) and limited by $p^\textrm{esc}_\textrm{max}$.

Hatchery-origin brood could be taken in two ways, either:

1. From fish in passage to spawning grounds, similar to natural-origin brood:

\begin{align}
\textrm{HOB}^\textrm{unmarked}_{y,a} &= p^\textrm{broodtake,unmarked}_y \times (1-m) \times E^\textrm{HO,avail}_{y,a}\\
\textrm{HOB}^\textrm{marked}_{y,a} &= p^\textrm{broodtake,marked}_y \times m \times E^\textrm{HO,avail}_{y,a}
(\#eq:HOB)
\end{align}

where some proportion $p^\textrm{broodtake,unmarked}$ of the available hatchery-origin escapement is taken:

\begin{equation}
E^\textrm{HO,avail}_{y,a} = E^\textrm{HO}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute} \times p^\textrm{esc}_\textrm{max}
(\#eq:HOB-avail)
\end{equation}

The mark rate $m$ is used to identify marked and unmarked hatchery-origin brood.

2. From fish "returning to the hatchery", e.g., through swim-in facilities or removal from spawning grounds:

Equation \@ref(eq:HOB) is used, but available escapement is defined as: 

\begin{equation}
E^\textrm{HO,avail}_{y,a} = p^\textrm{hatchery} \times E^\textrm{HO}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute} \times p^\textrm{esc}_\textrm{max}
(\#eq:HOB-avail2)
\end{equation}

Some fraction ($p^\textrm{hatchery}$) of the available hatchery-origin escapement returned to the hatchery $p^\textrm{hatchery}$, and a a subset is used for brood.

In either scenario for hatchery-origin brood, imported brood and strays may also be used:

\begin{align}
\textrm{Brood}^\textrm{import}_{y,a} &= p^\textrm{broodtake,marked}_y \sum_a \textrm{Brood}^\textrm{avail,import}_a\\
\textrm{HOB}^\textrm{stray}_{y,a} &= p^\textrm{broodtake,unmarked}_y \times \textrm{Stray}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute} \times p^\textrm{esc}_\textrm{max}
(\#eq:BroodtakeImportStray)
\end{align}

Annual strays and imported available brood are specified by the user.
In multi-population models, annual strays can be a state variable derived by stray rates and hatchery production in other systems (Appendix \@ref(app:multi)).

The proportions $p^\textrm{broodtake,unmarked}_y$ and $p^\textrm{broodtake,marked}_y$ specify the proportion of unmarked and marked fish used as brood.
They are solved annually to satisfy the following conditions:

\begin{align}
  \dfrac{\sum_a(\textrm{NOB}_{y,a} + \textrm{HOB}^\textrm{unmarked}_{y,a} + \textrm{HOB}^\textrm{stray}_{y,a})}{\sum_a(\textrm{NOB}_{y,a} + \textrm{HOB}^\textrm{unmarked}_{y,a} + \textrm{HOB}^\textrm{marked}_{y,a} + \textrm{HOB}^\textrm{stray}_{y,a} + \textrm{Brood}^\textrm{import}_{y,a})} = p^\textrm{NOB}_\textrm{target}\\
  0 < p^\textrm{broodtake,marked}_y \le 1\\
  0 < p^\textrm{broodtake,unmarked}_y \le p^\textrm{NOB}_\textrm{max}\\
  \textrm{Egg}_\textrm{y}^\textrm{NOB} + \textrm{Egg}_\textrm{y}^\textrm{HOB} + \textrm{Egg}_\textrm{y}^\textrm{import} + \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{stray}_y = \textrm{Egg}_\textrm{broodtake}
(\#eq:pBroodtake)
\end{align}

Annual egg production can fail to reach the target if there is insufficient unmarked escapement and $p^\textrm{broodtake,unmarked}_y = p^\textrm{NOB}_\textrm{max}$. 
In this case, the remaining deficit in egg production is met by increasing HOB (the realized $p^\textrm{NOB}$ can be lower than the target).

_Parameterization 2: Custom brood function_

In the custom brood function $f$, the user specifies the various types of brood taken from the available in-river return:

\begin{equation}
\begin{pmatrix}
\textrm{NOB}_{y,a}\\
\textrm{HOB}^\textrm{unmarked}_{y,a}\\
\textrm{HOB}^\textrm{marked}_{y,a}\\
\textrm{HOB}^\textrm{stray}_{y,a}
\end{pmatrix} = 
f\!\left(
\begin{matrix}
E^\textrm{NO,avail}_{y,a}\\
E^\textrm{HO,avail}_{y,a}\\
\textrm{Stray}_{y,a}\\
m
\end{matrix}
\right)
(\#eq:CustomBroodRule)
\end{equation}

In contrast to Parameterization 1, the custom function allows the user to specify age-selective brood rules.
The code also reduces brood to ensure the release target is not exceeded.

## In-river removals

After brood, further removals, e.g. as part of an in-river fishery or to manage natural spawning, is possible.
The in-river catch (IRC) or natural-origin fish is

\begin{equation}
\textrm{IRC}^\textrm{NO}_{y,a} = p^\textrm{IRC,NO}_y (E^\textrm{NO}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute} - \textrm{NOB}_{y,a})
(\#eq:IRC-NO)
\end{equation}

where the proportion removed $p^\textrm{IRC,NO}_y$ is either constant or a user-specified function $h_1$ of abundance and mark rate $m$:

$$
p^\textrm{IRC,NO}_y = h_1(E^\textrm{NO}_{y,a}, E^\textrm{HO}_{y,a}, m)
$$

If HOB are collected from fish on the way to spawning grounds, then:

\begin{equation}
\textrm{IRC}^\textrm{HO}_{y,a} = p^\textrm{IRC,HO}_y \times m (E^\textrm{HO}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute} - \textrm{HOB}_{y,a})
(\#eq:IRC-HO1)
\end{equation}

If HOB are collected from fish returning to the hatchery, then the hatchery-origin in-river catch is:

\begin{equation}
\textrm{IRC}^\textrm{HO}_{y,a} = p^\textrm{IRC,HO}_y \times m (1 - p^\textrm{hatchery}) E^\textrm{HO}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute}
(\#eq:IRC-HO2)
\end{equation}

The proportion removed $p^\textrm{IRC,HO}_y$ is either constant or a user-specified function $h_2$ of abundance and mark rate $m$:

$$
p^\textrm{IRC,HO}_y = h_2(E^\textrm{NO}_{y,a}, E^\textrm{HO}_{y,a}, m)
$$


## Spawners

Natural-origin spawners (NOS) is the escapement that survive return migration, are not used for brood, and are not removed from the spawning ground:

\begin{equation}
\textrm{NOS}_{y,a} = (1 - p^\textrm{IRC,NO}_y)(E^\textrm{NO}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute} - \textrm{NOB}_{y,a})
(\#eq:NOS)
\end{equation}

Hatchery-origin spawners (HOS) consist of fish local to the system and strays.
If HOB are collected from fish on the way to spawning grounds, then:

\begin{align}
\textrm{HOS}_{y,a} = (1 - p^\textrm{IRC,HOS}_y \times m) (E^\textrm{HO}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute} - \textrm{HOB}_{y,a}) + (\textrm{Stray}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute} - \textrm{HOB}^\textrm{stray}_{y,a})
(\#eq:HOS1)
\end{align}

If HOB are collected from fish returning to the hatchery, then the hatchery-origin spawners is:

\begin{equation}
\textrm{HOS}_{y,a} = (1 - p^\textrm{IRC,HOS}_y \times m) (1 - p^\textrm{hatchery}) E^\textrm{HO}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute} + (\textrm{Stray}_{y,a} \times s_\textrm{enroute} - \textrm{HOB}^\textrm{stray}_{y,a})
(\#eq:HOS2)
\end{equation}

## Natural-origin juvenile production

This section describes the calculation of natural-origin juveniles of the next generation from the spawner abundance in the previous year.

We consider natural production in the absence of fitness effects arising from hatchery production. 
Modified equations accounting for fitness are described in Appendix \@ref(app:fitness).

The outmigrating juveniles of the next generation is predicted from the spawners from the previous year.
Two parameterizations are possible: (1) a single density-dependent stock-recruit relationship (SRR) is used model egg-juvenile survival, or (2) a series of density-dependent functions models survival at intermittent freshwater life stages.

_Parameterization 1: Juvenile production from single stock-recruit relationship_

Egg production is calculated as

\begin{align}
\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_y &= \sum_a\textrm{NOS}_{y,a} \times p^\textrm{female}_a \times \textrm{Fec}_a\\
\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_y &= \sum_a\textrm{HOS}_{\textrm{eff}y,a} \times p^\textrm{female}_a \times \textrm{Fec}_a
(\#eq:SpawnOutput)
\end{align}

where $\textrm{HOS}_{\textrm{eff}} = \gamma \times \textrm{HOS}$, $p^\textrm{female}$ is the proportion female, $\textrm{Fec}$ is fecundity, and superscripts denote the parentage of the progeny.

The smolt production is interpreted as the age-1 abundance in the following year $y+1$.
If the smolt production is calculated from the Ricker stock-recruit relationship, effectively over the entire freshwater life stage:

\begin{align}
  \textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{NOS}_{y+1} &= \alpha \times \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_{y}\times\exp(-\beta[\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_{y} + \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_{y}])\\
  \textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{HOS}_{y+1} &= \alpha \times \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_{y}\times\exp(-\beta[\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_{y} + \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_{y}])\\
(\#eq:SmoltProdRicker)
\end{align}

The density-independent component of the survival equation is controlled by $\alpha$ and the density-dependent component of survival is controlled by $\beta$ and scaled by the total egg production, where

\begin{align}
  \alpha &= \kappa/\phi\\
  \beta &= 1/{E_\textrm{max}}\\
  E_\textrm{max} &= S_\textrm{max} \times \phi/\tau\\
  \phi &= \sum_a\left(\prod_{i=1}^{a-1}\exp(-M^\textrm{NOS}_i)(1-r_i)\right)\times r_a \times p^\textrm{female}_a \times \textrm{Fec}_a\\
  \tau &= \sum_a\left(\prod_{i=1}^{a-1}\exp(-M^\textrm{NOS}_i)(1-r_i)\right)\times r_a \times p^\textrm{female}_a
(\#eq:RickerParameters)
\end{align}

$\kappa$ is the productivity (returns/spawner), $\phi$ is the egg production per smolt at replacement over the lifetime of a brood year, and $\tau$ is the female spawner per smolt at replacement. 
Salmon populations are typically modeled by a SRR that predicts the recruitment (returning adults) from the number of spawners. Parameters $\tau$ and $\phi$ allow conversion of a spawner-return SRR to an equivalent egg-juvenile SRR that predicts the returns/spawner specified in $\kappa$.

Alternatively, the age-1 smolt production can be predicted from the Beverton-Holt stock-recruit relationship as:

\begin{align}
\textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{NOS}_{y+1} &= \frac{\alpha \times \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_{y}}{1 + \beta(\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_{y} + \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_{y})}\\
\textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{HOS}_{y+1} &= \frac{\alpha \times \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_{y}}{1 + \beta(\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_{y} + \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_{y})}
\end{align}

where

\begin{align}
  \alpha &= \kappa/\phi\\
  \beta &= \alpha/{C_\textrm{egg-smolt}}
(\#eq:BHParameters)
\end{align}

_Parameterization 2: Juvenile production from stage-specific survival_

The spawner to juvenile life stages can also be modeled through a series of density-dependent functions, following the general approach of @jorgensen2021.  
Four relationships are modeled:

1. Pre-spawn mortality
2. Egg incubation mortality
3. Egg emergence to fry mortality
4. Fry to smolt mortality

Survival is modeled through either a Beverton-Holt or hockey-stick function that predicts survivors from the abundance at the beginning of the life stage (Figure \@ref(fig:habitat-ex)).

Alternative scenarios with changes in productivity or capacity parameters can be used to evaluate changes in life stage survival from habitat improvement or mitigation measures as part of a management strategy, or from climate regimes (low productivity vs. high productivity, or low capacity vs. high capacity).
An increase in capacity can arise from restoration which increases the area of suitable habitat.
An increase in productivity can arise from improvement in habitat, e.g., sediment quality.
Year-specific deviations can be used to simulate stochasticity in survival.

These relationships are intended to be parameterized by empirical data or expert judgement. 
Approaches such as HARP [@beechie2021] and CEMPRA [@bayly2025] can inform productivity and capacity parameters across these life stages as quantitative relationships between habitat variables.

```{r habitat-ex, fig.cap="Example set of life stage density-dependent relationships: (1) density-independent pre-spawn mortality of 5% (95% survival), (2) density-dependent egg incubation mortality relationship (maximum survival of 80% and 2 million eggs as the capacity), (3) density-independent egg-fry survival of 1, and (4) density-dependent fry-smolt survival (maximum of 20% and 10,000 smolts as the capacity). Dashed lines indicate the one-to-one line (100% survival)."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path("figures", "habitat.png"))
```

_Stage 1: Pre-spawn mortality_

Pre-spawn (ps) mortality can occur, where the surviving spawners $\widetilde{\textrm{NOS}}_y$ and $\widetilde{\textrm{HOS}}_y$ are:

\begin{align}
\widetilde{\textrm{NOS}}_y &= \frac{P^\textrm{ps} \times 
\textrm{NOS}_y}{1 + \frac{P^\textrm{ps}}{C^\textrm{ps}}(\textrm{NOS}_y + \textrm{HOS}_y)}\\
\widetilde{\textrm{HOS}}_y &= \frac{P^\textrm{ps} \times 
\textrm{HOS}_y}{1 + \frac{P^\textrm{ps}}{C^\textrm{ps}}(\textrm{NOS}_y + \textrm{HOS}_y)}
(\#eq:PrespawnMortHabitatBH)
\end{align}

where productivity $P$ is the maximum survival as spawner numbers approaches zero and $C$ is the asymptotic number of spawners, i.e., spawner capacity.

The alternative hockey-stick formulation is 

\begin{align}
\widetilde{\textrm{NOS}}_y &= \textrm{min}(P^\textrm{ps} \times \textrm{NOS}_y, (\frac{\textrm{NOS}_y}{\textrm{NOS}_y + \textrm{HOS}_y}) C^\textrm{ps})\\
\widetilde{\textrm{HOS}}_y &= \textrm{min}(P^\textrm{ps} \times \textrm{HOS}_y, (\frac{\textrm{HOS}_y}{\textrm{NOS}_y + \textrm{HOS}_y}) C^\textrm{ps})
(\#eq:HockeyStick)
\end{align}

with similar parameterizations for subsequent life stages (not further described below). 

_Stage 2: Egg incubation mortality_

The initial egg production is calculated after pre-spawn mortality:

\begin{align}
\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_y &= \sum_a\widetilde{\textrm{NOS}}_{y,a} \times p^\textrm{female}_a \times \textrm{Fec}_a\\
\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_y &= \sum_a\widetilde{\textrm{HOS}}_{\textrm{eff}y,a} \times p^\textrm{female}_a \times \textrm{Fec}_a
(\#eq:EggProdHabitat)
\end{align}

Second, the surviving egg production ($\widetilde{\textrm{Egg}}_y$) can be reduced from the initial spawning output ($\textrm{Egg}_y$) due to incubation mortality. With a Beverton-Holt function:

\begin{align}
\widetilde{\textrm{Egg}}^\textrm{NOS}_y &= \frac{P^\textrm{inc} \times 
\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_y}{1 + \frac{P^\textrm{inc}}{C^\textrm{inc}}(\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_y + \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_y)}\\
\widetilde{\textrm{Egg}}^\textrm{HOS}_y &= \frac{P^\textrm{inc} \times 
\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_y}{1 + \frac{P^\textrm{inc}}{C^\textrm{inc}}(\textrm{Egg}^\textrm{NOS}_y + \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{HOS}_y)}
(\#eq:EggIncMortHabitat)
\end{align}

where productivity $P$ is the maximum survival as spawning output approaches zero and $C$ is the asymptotic production (egg capacity).

_Stage 3: Egg to fry mortality_

Fry production is modeled as:

\begin{align}
\textrm{Fry}^\textrm{NOS}_{y+1} &= \frac{P^\textrm{egg-fry} \times
\widetilde{\textrm{Egg}}^\textrm{NOS}_y}{1 + \frac{P^\textrm{egg-fry}}{C^\textrm{egg-fry}}(\widetilde{\textrm{Egg}}^\textrm{NOS}_y + \widetilde{\textrm{Egg}}^\textrm{HOS}_y)} \times \varepsilon^\textrm{egg-fry}_y\\
\textrm{Fry}^\textrm{HOS}_{y+1} &= \frac{P^\textrm{egg-fry} \times
\widetilde{\textrm{Egg}}^\textrm{HOS}_y}{1 + \frac{P^\textrm{egg-fry}}{C^\textrm{egg-fry}}(\widetilde{\textrm{Egg}}^\textrm{NOS}_y + \widetilde{\textrm{Egg}}^\textrm{HOS}_y)} \times \varepsilon^\textrm{egg-fry}_y
(\#eq:FryProdHabitat)
\end{align}

where $\varepsilon^\textrm{egg-fry}_y$ is a year-specific deviation in survival. They can be modeled as a function of a proposed time series of environmental variables $\eta$, for example, $\varepsilon^\textrm{egg-fry}_y = \prod_j f(\eta_{y,j})$ or $\varepsilon^\textrm{egg-fry}_y = \sum_j f(\eta_{y,j})$.

_Stage 4: Fry to smolt mortality_

The last freshwater life stage with smolt production is modeled as:

\begin{align}
\textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{NOS}_y &= \frac{P^\textrm{fry-smolt} \times
\textrm{Fry}^\textrm{NOS}_y}{1 + \frac{P^\textrm{fry-smolt}}{C^\textrm{fry-smolt}}(\textrm{Fry}^\textrm{NOS}_y + \textrm{Fry}^\textrm{HOS}_y)} \times \varepsilon^\textrm{fry-smolt}_y\\
\textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{HOS}_y &= \frac{P^\textrm{fry-smolt} \times
\textrm{Fry}^\textrm{HOS}_y}{1 + \frac{P^\textrm{fry-smolt}}{C^\textrm{fry-smolt}}(\textrm{Fry}^\textrm{NOS}_y + \textrm{Fry}^\textrm{HOS}_y)} \times \varepsilon^\textrm{fry-smolt}_y
(\#eq:SmoltProdHabitat)
\end{align}

\textrm{Fry}^\textrm{NOS}_y}{1 + \frac{P^\textrm{fry-smolt}}{C^\textrm{fry-smolt}}(\textrm{Fry}^\textrm{NOS}_y + \textrm{Fry}^\textrm{HOS}_y + n^\textrm{subyearling}_y + n^\textrm{yearling}_y)} \times \varepsilon^\textrm{fry-smolt}_y\\

## Hatchery-origin juvenile production_

The hatchery egg production is

\begin{align}
\textrm{Egg}_\textrm{y}^\textrm{NOB} &= \sum_a \textrm{NOB}_{y,a} \times s^\textrm{prespawn} \times p^\textrm{female,brood}_a \times \textrm{Fec}^\textrm{brood}_a\\
\textrm{Egg}_\textrm{y}^\textrm{HOB} &= \sum_a (\textrm{HOB}^\textrm{marked}_{y,a} + \textrm{HOB}^\textrm{unmarked}_{y,a}) \times s^\textrm{prespawn} \times p^\textrm{female,brood}_a \times \textrm{Fec}^\textrm{brood}_a\\
\textrm{Egg}_\textrm{y}^\textrm{import} &= \sum_a \textrm{Brood}^\textrm{import}_{y,a} \times s^\textrm{prespawn} \times p^\textrm{female,brood}_a \times \textrm{Fec}^\textrm{brood}_a\\
\textrm{Egg}_\textrm{y}^\textrm{stray} &= \sum_a \textrm{HOB}^\textrm{stray}_{y,a} \times s^\textrm{prespawn} \times p^\textrm{female,brood}_a \times \textrm{Fec}^\textrm{brood}_a\\
(\#eq:EggProd)
\end{align}

where brood is subject to a survival term $s^\textrm{prespawn}$ prior to egg production.

After the hatchery egg production is calculated, the production of yearlings and subyearlings is calculated to ensure the annual ratio is equal to the target ratio. To do so, the parameter $p^\textrm{egg,yearling}_y$ is solved subject to the following conditions:

\begin{align}
    \textrm{Egg}_\textrm{brood,y} &= \textrm{Egg}_\textrm{y}^\textrm{NOB} + \textrm{Egg}_\textrm{y}^\textrm{HOB} + \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{import}_y + \textrm{Egg}^\textrm{stray}_y (\#eq:Eggsum) \\
  n^\textrm{yearling}_{y+1} &= p^\textrm{egg,yearling}_y \times \textrm{Egg}_\textrm{brood,y} \times s^\textrm{yearling} (\#eq:YearlingTarget) \\
  n^\textrm{subyearling}_{y+1} &= (1 - p^\textrm{egg,yearling}_y) \times \textrm{Egg}_\textrm{brood,y} \times s^\textrm{subyearling} (\#eq:SubyearlingTarget)\\
  \frac{n^\textrm{yearling}_y}{n^\textrm{subyearling}_y + n^\textrm{yearling}_y} &= \frac{n^\textrm{yearling}_\textrm{target}}{n^\textrm{subyearling}_\textrm{target} + n^\textrm{yearling}_\textrm{target}}
  (\#eq:ProdYearSubYear)
\end{align}

Assuming no density-dependent competition with natural-origin juveniles, the outmigrating releases ("smolt releases") is

$$
\textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{Rel}_{y+1} = n^\textrm{subyearling}_{y+1} + n^\textrm{yearling}_{y+1}
$$

<!--
With competition, the outmigrating abundance is:

$$
\textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{Rel}_{y+1} = \alpha \times (n^\textrm{subyearling}_{y+1} + n^\textrm{yearling}_{y+1}) \times \exp(-\beta(\textrm{Fry}^\textrm{NOS}_{y+1} + \textrm{Fry}^\textrm{HOS}_{y+1} + n^\textrm{subyearling}_{y+1} + n^\textrm{yearling}_{y+1}))
$$

or

$$
\textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{Rel}_{y+1} = \frac{\alpha \times (n^\textrm{subyearling}_{y+1} + n^\textrm{yearling}_{y+1})}{1 + \beta(\textrm{Fry}^\textrm{NOS}_{y+1} + \textrm{Fry}^\textrm{HOS}_{y+1} + n^\textrm{subyearling}_{y+1} + n^\textrm{yearling}_{y+1})}
$$

## Next year's juvenile abundance

The projection continues in the next year $y+1$ by setting the age-1 juvenile abundance as $N^\textrm{juv,NO}_{y+1,a=1} = \textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{NOS}_{y+1} + \textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{HOS}_{y+1}$ and $N^\textrm{juv,HO}_{y+1,a=1} = \textrm{Smolt}^\textrm{Rel}_{y+1}$.

# DERIVED QUANTITIES

Once the projection completes, several derived quantities of interest related to hatchery production are calculated.

## pHOS, pNOB

The proportion of spawners that are hatchery-origin (pHOS, pHOSeff) and the proportion of brood that is natural-origin (pNOB) are calculated as:

\begin{align}
 \textrm{pHOS}_{y} &= \dfrac{\sum_a \textrm{HOS}_{y,a} \times \textrm{Fec}_{y,a}}{\sum_a(\textrm{HOS}_{y,a} + \textrm{NOS}_{y,a}) \textrm{Fec}_{y,a}} (\#eq:pHOS)\\
 \textrm{pHOSeff}_{y} &= \dfrac{\sum_a \gamma \times \textrm{HOS}_{y,a} \times \textrm{Fec}_{y,a}}{\sum_a(\gamma \times \textrm{HOS}_{y,a} + \textrm{NOS}_{y,a}) \textrm{Fec}_{y,a}} (\#eq:pHOSeff)\\
 \textrm{pNOB}_{y} &= \dfrac{\sum_a \gamma \times \textrm{HOS}_{y,a} \times \textrm{Fec}_{y,a}}{\sum_a(\gamma \times \textrm{HOS}_{y,a} + \textrm{NOS}_{y,a}) \textrm{Fec}_{y,a}} (\#eq:pNOB)
\end{align}

Equations \@ref(eq:pHOS)--\@ref(eq:pNOB) are weighted by age class fecundity, accounting for older age classes with larger contributions to the egg production.

## Wild salmon

With single brood-year returns, the proportion of wild salmon, natural-origin spawners whose parents were also natural spawners, has been calculated as

\begin{equation}
  \textrm{pWILD}_g = (1 - \textrm{pHOS}_g) \times
  \dfrac{(1 - \textrm{pHOS}_{g-1})^2}
  {(1 - \textrm{pHOS}_{g-1})^2 + 2 \gamma \times \textrm{pHOS}_{g-1}(1 - \textrm{pHOS}_{g-1}) +
  \gamma^2 \textrm{pHOS}_{g-1}^2}
  (\#eq:pWild)
\end{equation}

where $\textrm{pHOS} = \textrm{HOS}/(\textrm{HOS} + \textrm{NOS})$.

The first term of Equation \@ref(eq:pWild) is the proportion of natural spawners in the current generation $g$.
The ratio comprising the second term discounts the proportion of the current generation to include natural-origin spawners whose parents were both natural-origin spawners.
Assuming non-assortative mating, the three terms in the denominator gives the composition of generation $g$ whose parents who are both natural-origin, mixed origin (one parent in natural-origin and the other is hatchery-origin), and both hatchery-origin.

In salmonMSE, to generalize for mixed-brood year spawners, we calculate the probability weighted across brood-years and age class fecundity:

\begin{equation}
\textrm{pWILD}_y = \sum_a \left(\dfrac{\textrm{NOS}_{y,a}}{\sum_{a'}(\textrm{NOS}_{y,a'} + \textrm{HOS}_{y,a'})} \times
\dfrac{(\sum_{a'} \textrm{pNOS}_{y-a,a'})^2}{(\sum_{a'} \textrm{pNOS}_{y-a,a'})^2 + 2 \gamma \times (\sum_{a'}\textrm{pNOS}_{y-a,a'})(\sum_{a'}\textrm{pHOS}_{y-a,a'}) + \gamma^2 (\sum_{a'}\textrm{pHOS}_{y-a,a'})^2}\right)
(\#eq:pWildMixed)
\end{equation}

where 

\begin{align}
  \textrm{pNOS}_{y,a} &= \dfrac{\textrm{Fec}_a \times \textrm{NOS}_{y,a}}{\sum_a{\textrm{Fec}_a (\textrm{NOS}_{y,a}} + \textrm{HOS}_{y,a})} \\
  \textrm{pHOS}_{y,a} &= \dfrac{\textrm{Fec}_a \times \textrm{HOS}_{y,a}}{\sum_a{\textrm{Fec}_a (\textrm{NOS}_{y,a}} + \textrm{HOS}_{y,a})}\\
  (\#eq:pWildMixed)
\end{align}

In equation \@ref(eq:pWildMixed), the probability of finding a wild spawner in year $y$ is the sum of probabilities of finding a wild salmon over all ages.
For each age $a$, the first ratio is the probability of finding a natural-origin spawner in year $y$.
The second ratio is the probability of mating success from two parental natural-origin spawners in year $y-a$ using a Punnett square, assuming non-assortative mating across age and origin.
The summation across dummy age variable $a'$ calculates the total proportion of spawners in a given year.

## PNI

PNI (proportionate natural influence) is an approximation of the rate of gene flow from the hatchery to the natural environment, calculated for the progeny in year $y+1$ from the parental composition of year $y$:

\begin{equation}
 \textrm{PNI}_{y+1} = \dfrac{\textrm{pNOB}_y}{\textrm{pNOB}_y + \textrm{pHOSeff}_y}
 (\#eq:PNI)
\end{equation}

Generally, a combination of minimizing hatchery releases, increasing natural broodtake, and reducing the number hatchery origin spawners maintains high PNI, i.e., low rate of gene flow from the hatchery to natural environment.

If there is no natural-origin brood, e.g., brood is imported or there are only strays, then PNI is calculated with equation 6 of @withler2018:

\begin{equation}
 \textrm{PNI}_{y+1} = \dfrac{h^2}{h^2 + (1 - h^2 + \omega^2) \textrm{pHOSeff}_y}
 (\#eq:AllImportPNI)
\end{equation}

where $h$ and $\omega$ are defined in Appendix \@ref(app:fitness).
